During the height of the trade war between Trump and China, when tariffs were being imposed almost every week, companies like Logitech immediately raised the prices of their products sold in the US significantly.

Earlier this year, the US Supreme Court ruled these tariffs illegal and ordered refunds to manufacturers. Yet to date, no company has been seen passing the refunds on to consumers, and class-action lawsuits have been filed demanding this be corrected...

The Trump tariff saga

Trump made a big deal last year about the US trade deficit with China, apparently fantasising that slapping hefty tariffs on Chinese-made products would force companies like Apple to move their production lines back to the US.

Of course, this never happened. The US simply lacks the manufacturing infrastructure, expertise, and cheap labour to support large brands producing consumer electronics at that scale.

Trump kept claiming it was China paying the tariffs, but the reality is that US brands absorbed the cost when importing finished Chinese goods, then passed it on to consumers through higher prices. Tariff rates at the peak of the saga soared as high as 145%.

Take Logitech as an example: the company raised prices on roughly half of its products by up to 25%.

Consumers deserve refunds

The US Supreme Court ultimately ruled that Trump had no authority to impose these tariffs unilaterally, and ordered that the money already paid by US companies must be refunded. The refund process is currently underway.

The problem is that these costs were ultimately borne by consumers through higher prices, yet the affected companies have still not announced any plans to refund their customers.

The law firm CPM has already filed a class-action lawsuit against Logitech, demanding refunds for consumers who paid the inflated prices during the period the tariffs were in effect.

9to5Mac's take

The principle here is indisputable: companies paid the tariffs, passed the extra cost on to customers, and are now getting the money back from the government. Morally speaking, they ought to return that money to consumers who bought their products during this period.

In practical terms, however, this would be extremely difficult. Logitech would have to identify every single transaction conducted through its vast network of third-party retailers, record the actual amounts consumers paid, and calculate what proportion of that was attributable to tariffs.

Even if the lawsuit ultimately succeeds, it could set a rather interesting precedent — though it must be noted that in class-action suits, the biggest winners are usually the lawyers, with ordinary consumers typically receiving only negligible amounts.
